summary: Specifies the Open Shortest Path First routing protocol, an interior gateway protocol that spreads routing information inside one autonomous system. It is based on the link-state approach and not the distance-vector one. It was replaced by RFC 1247.

plainLanguage.summary: OSPF is an internal routing protocol that lets routers build a shared map of an Autonomous System. Each router calculates shortest paths from itself using that map.

subtitle: Specifies a link-state routing protocol for routers within one Autonomous System.

tldr.problem: The RFC describes a need for a routing protocol that responds quickly to topology changes while using small amounts of routing traffic.
tldr.mechanism: OSPF routers flood local link state, build a topology database and calculate shortest-path trees; areas limit the spread of detailed topology information.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1131 specifies OSPF and was obsoleted by RFC 1247.

today: RFC 1131 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 1247. It specifies OSPF version 1.

sections.title: What OSPF Does
sections.content:
OSPF, or Open Shortest Path First, is an Internal Gateway Protocol that distributes routing information among routers in one Autonomous System. It is based on link-state technology rather than the Bellman-Ford base used by traditional Internet routing protocols.

OSPF routes packets using the destination IP address and IP Type of Service. It is designed to react to topology changes while keeping routing protocol traffic small.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF shares routing information among routers in one Autonomous System. It uses link-state information to compute routes.

sections.title: The Topological Database
sections.content:
Each router maintains a database describing the Autonomous System as a directed graph of routers and networks. A router distributes its local state by flooding link state advertisements. Routers in an area have identical area topology databases.

Each router calculates a shortest-path tree with itself as the root. The tree gives routes to destinations, and externally derived routing information appears as leaves.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers in an area share the same description of its topology. Each router uses that database to build shortest paths from itself.

sections.title: Areas and the Backbone
sections.content:
OSPF allows contiguous networks and hosts to be grouped into areas. Each area runs a separate copy of the basic SPF algorithm and has its own topology database. The area's detailed topology is hidden from routers outside it, reducing routing traffic.

Routing between areas uses the backbone. The backbone must be contiguous; the RFC describes virtual links as a way for an administrator to restore connectivity when needed. Area border routers summarize information from attached areas for distribution through the backbone.
sections.plainLanguage: Areas limit how much topology detail routers need to exchange. Inter-area routes use the backbone and summarized information.
